summary: Redwood AE+SE walked AtlasFin through the Redwood Console tracing and error analysis features, request logs, and debugging flows. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated for a high-throughput latency-sensitive fraud detection flow. Key asks: SOC2/Security docs, a benchmarking run with AtlasFin sample payloads, cost estimates for Dedicated vs Hosted, and a POC kickoff next week.
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Alex from Redwood. Today Priya and I will walk through the Console tracing and error analysis features, show request logs, and talk through debugging flows.
[00:15] Tom Wilson: Thanks, Alex. Quick note, we have Maya and Sam on — we mostly care about tail latency and error spikes impacting inference for fraud detection.
[00:30] Priya Patel: Great, Tom. We'll start with a quick orientation and then jump into a live demo. If anything is unclear, interrupt.
[00:45] Maya Rivera: Sounds good. Also security — we're going to need SOC 2 and KMS details.
[00:55] Alex Chen: Yep we'll cover that at the end and I'll share docs.
[01:05] Priya Patel: (screen shares) Opening Redwood Console, home dashboard. We'll go to the Traces tab — note this is tied to request IDs and the route/model you call.
[01:30] Priya Patel: Here's a sample trace, you'll see spans for routing, queuing, model loading, and token generation. The timeline shows per-span latency; you can zoom into a single request.
[01:55] Sam Lee: Is that the KV cache span?
[02:05] Priya Patel: Yes, you'll see a "K V cache" span — sometimes the transcriber in our internal logs does the spacing oddly — it represents the KV cache lookup. If the KV hit rate is low you will see a larger model computation span.
[02:30] Tom Wilson: Can we correlate traces to request payloads?
[02:40] Priya Patel: Absolutely — request logs are linked. Click the request ID and the right pane shows request/response, headers, prompt, and environment tags (region, model variant, quantization profile).
[03:00] Priya Patel: Note: for privacy we can mask PII in logs or configure retention settings per-account.
[03:20] Maya Rivera: How long do logs stay by default?
[03:25] Alex Chen: Hosted tier has 30 days standard, Dedicated can increase retention and we have add-on log retention packages. We'll include specifics in the doc.
[03:40] Priya Patel: Back to traces — we also show error counters and a histogram of error types by route. If you click an error cluster, it surfaces common stack traces and the failing request samples.
[04:05] Tom Wilson: Do you capture model-side errors vs infrastructure errors?
[04:12] Priya Patel: We tag errors by layer: infra (OOM, node failure), runtime (kernel failures, quantization mismatch), and model (generation errors, truncated outputs). There's some occasional mislabeling in auto-parse but it's useful for triage.
[04:40] Priya Patel: For debugging flows, we recommend these steps: 1) Locate high-latency traces, 2) open the request log, 3) check KV cache hit/miss, 4) inspect model variant and quantization profile, 5) re-run the request in a sandbox with increased logging.
[05:10] Sam Lee: Can we replay traffic or dump to a staging endpoint?
[05:20] Priya Patel: Yes, you can export a set of request logs as a replay bundle and run them against a Dedicated pool or a private endpoint. We provide a replay runner CLI.
[05:35] Tom Wilson: What about sampling — do you sample traces? We have a lot of QPS.
[05:45] Alex Chen: We do adaptive sampling: more aggressive for normal requests, full capture for errors and for configured guardrails. You can also set route-level sampling policy in the Console.
[06:05] Maya Rivera: How do rollouts and fallbacks show up in traces?
[06:15] Priya Patel: Good question. If a request is routed to a fallback model or region, the trace includes routing decision spans and the policy tag. You can filter traces by policy or by model variant.
[06:35] Tom Wilson: You mentioned quantization profiles — are those visible per-request?
[06:45] Priya Patel: Yes, the request metadata shows the quantization and MLIR/kernel path we used if available — helpful when diagnosing accuracy regressions after quant changes.
[07:05] Alex Chen: A common ask is tying cost to traces — the Console can show token counts and estimated cost per-request in the request detail panel.
[07:25] Sam Lee: Nice, that will help explain spikes to finance.
[07:30] Priya Patel: Moving to Error Analysis view — this aggregates failed requests by signature and root cause. Here you can pin a representative request to a regression watch.
[07:50] Maya Rivera: Can we set alerts?
[07:55] Alex Chen: Yes, alerting via webhook, email, or PagerDuty for error rates, latency SLO breaches, or specific trace anomalies.
[08:10] Tom Wilson: Security question — do you store logs encrypted at rest with customer KMS options?
[08:18] Alex Chen: Yes, Dedicated and Private offer customer-managed KMS/HSM. Hosted supports AWS KMS-managed keys as an option for enterprise accounts. We'll send the architecture doc.
[08:35] Priya Patel: Demo note — sometimes you may see small transcription errors in labels (e.g., SAML becomes Sam L) — ignore those, they're from auto-labeling not the platform.
[08:55] Tom Wilson: On performance: our batch sizes are small but latency budget is tight. We want the 99th percentile under 250ms for short prompts.
[09:10] Priya Patel: For that profile we typically recommend a Dedicated pool with hot model priming and KV caching enabled. In Console you can configure priming warmers and view cold-start vs warm latency in traces.
[09:35] Sam Lee: Can we see warmers run?
[09:40] Priya Patel: Yes, warmers are an instrumented task — traces show warmer executions and you can correlate them with the subsequent request's cold-start reduction.
[10:00] Alex Chen: Let's run a quick live filter: show traces for route /api/v1/infer where 99th latency > 200ms in the last 24h. (screen shows list) Here's a cluster of failures around 03:20 UTC.
[10:25] Priya Patel: Opening one — you'll see a long kernel selection span, and an infra retry. The error rate increased during a driver upgrade window; our Smart Routing had some fallbacks.
[10:45] Tom Wilson: Could we have seen that earlier?
[10:50] Priya Patel: With anomaly detection enabled we will alert on unusual divergence in span duration distributions. We also have a trace-based histogram alert.
[11:05] Maya Rivera: For the POC, we want to validate throughput at our peak 200 rps and measure tail latency.
[11:15] Alex Chen: Priya will run a benchmark using your payloads against a Dedicated pool and provide a report with per-span breakdown, token cost estimates, and suggested optimizations like batching or quantization tweaks.
[11:35] Priya Patel: Quick note on request logs: you can export CSV or JSON bundles for compliance reviews. For high-volume customers we do S3 export hooks.
[11:55] Sam Lee: Are there RBAC controls for who can view traces and PII?
[12:05] Alex Chen: Yes RBAC with role scoping. You can restrict who can view request/response content, who can export logs, and who can change routing policies.
[12:25] Tom Wilson: Any limitations around private deployment? We have to be air-gapped for some clients.
[12:35] Alex Chen: Our Private deployment supports air-gapped installs with a customer-managed control plane; there are additional operational requirements. We'll put details in the Private deployment checklist.
[12:55] Maya Rivera: Can Priya show the request replay flow real quick?
[13:00] Priya Patel: Sure — select requests, click Export -> Replay bundle, then from CLI run redwood replay --bundle <bundle> --endpoint <staging>. It will replay with timing and concurrency controls.
[13:25] Sam Lee: Does replay keep original timestamps or adjust them?
[13:30] Priya Patel: You can preserve timestamps or replay in wall-clock relative timing. Also you can throttle concurrency.
[13:50] Alex Chen: Moving to integrations — Console ties to our observability hooks so you can forward traces to Datadog or BigQuery for custom analysis.
[14:10] Tom Wilson: We use Datadog already, that's helpful.
[14:15] Priya Patel: Last section: debugging a model regression — we'll use Error Analysis to compare a baseline prompt set to a new deployment. You can set evaluation prompts and watch quality regressions surfaced by diffs in outputs.
[14:40] Maya Rivera: Are model diffs automated?
[14:45] Priya Patel: They can be; Redwood Optimize can run scheduled evaluations against pinned prompts and alert on quality regressions.
[15:00] Tom Wilson: Great. What's the expected timeline for the POC?
[15:05] Alex Chen: If we get the sample payloads this week, we can kick off the benchmark early next week and aim for a POC config and estimate by 12/15.
[15:20] Maya Rivera: Okay, we'll share payloads and also a typical traffic day.
[15:30] Alex Chen: Recap of next steps: I'll send SOC2 and security architecture, Priya will run benchmark and share runbook, customer to share payloads. We'll set POC kickoff.
[15:45] Tom Wilson: Sounds good. Thanks Alex, Priya.
[15:50] Priya Patel: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with a calendar invite for the kickoff.
[16:00] (call ends)

Notes: transcription contains occasional mis-hearings (SAML -> Sam L, KV cache sometimes split). The demo showed how to trace routing decisions, view per-request token cost, link request logs, export replay bundles, and configure alerts.
